message.content:
The Greyhound coughed to a halt, spitting me out onto the cracked pavement of Havenwood’s town square. It was exactly as I remembered: a single, slightly lopsided oak tree dominating the space, the faded brick of the town hall behind it, and the lingering scent of pine and damp earth. Ten years. Ten years since I’d last inhaled this particular brand of small-town tranquility, ten years since I’d considered myself anything other than a runaway. 

Honestly, I wasn't sure why I’d agreed to this. My life in Chicago was…comfortable. Predictable. I had a decent job editing marketing copy, a tiny but charming apartment overflowing with succulents, and a reliable routine that involved yoga on Tuesdays and sushi on Fridays. But a frantic phone call from Leo Harding, of all people, had pulled me back. He needed help. Apparently, opening a cafe was harder than it looked.

Leo. Just the name brought a rush of memories – awkward school dances, shared lunches in the cafeteria, the way his brow furrowed when he was concentrating on a particularly difficult physics problem. We hadn’t been close, not really. Just…classmates. Friendly acquaintances. The kind of people you nodded to in the hallway and occasionally exchanged a few words with. Now, here he was, asking for my assistance in bringing his dream of “The Daily Grind” to life. 

The cafe itself was located in the old Miller's Hardware building, a surprisingly spacious spot with large windows that looked out onto the square. Leo met me at the curb, a whirlwind of nervous energy and flour dust. He was taller than I remembered, broader too, and his usual boyish grin seemed stretched thin with worry. "Mina! You made it! Thank God." He practically dragged me inside, a chaotic tableau of mismatched chairs, half-painted walls, and the aroma of strong coffee struggling to overcome the lingering smell of sawdust. 

"It's…a lot," I observed, taking in the scene. Boxes overflowed with supplies, a single barista machine sat gleaming on the counter, and a stack of menus lay scattered on a nearby table. Leo just laughed, a slightly hysterical sound. "Tell me about it. I thought it would be all sunshine and lattes, but it's mostly just sunshine and stress." 

He gestured around the room, launching into a rapid-fire explanation of his plans – artisanal pastries, locally sourced coffee beans, a cozy atmosphere perfect for reading and conversation. It was ambitious, bordering on insane, but I could see the passion in his eyes, the genuine desire to create something special. Maybe, just maybe, helping him wouldn't be so bad after all. Maybe a little small-town tranquility was exactly what I needed.



The first order of business, according to Leo, was unpacking boxes. Lots and lots of boxes.
